title: Montreal police officer to be charged with manslaughter in Montreal North shooting
article: More than a year after a man died after being shot by police with a rubber bullet in Montreal North, a Montreal police officer is being charged with manslaughter.
Bony Jean-Pierre, a 46-year-old black man, was shot during a drug raid gone wrong at an apartment complex on March 31, 2016. He died a few days later from his injuries.

After reviewing the evidence, Quebec's Crown prosecutor's office (DPCP) announced Wednesday it has decided to charge Montreal police officer Christian Gilbert with manslaughter. Gilbert will appear in court on July 6.

The DPCP said it would not be commenting on its decision, as did the Montreal police department. Sentences for manslaughter in which a firearm is used range from a minimum of four years in prison to a life sentence.

Jean-Pierre's death led to unrest in the borough - including a violent night of protest during which the local police station was vandalized - and renewed calls for improved race relations in Montreal North.

The protest had coincided with a vigil to commemorate the life of Fredy Villanueva, an 18-year-old who was shot and killed by police in the borough in 2008. No criminal charges were ever filed against the officers involved.
The news of charges being laid in Jean-Pierre's death - nearly 14 months after the fact - came as a slight relief Wednesday to those who had been pushing for answers for the last year.

"In the Villanueva case, nine years later, we're still fighting and trying to place a criminal complaint against the officer. That's what we were expecting to have to do here, too," said Will Prosper, a documentary filmmaker and community activist who says he has spoken with people who were in the apartment during the raid.
"We weren't expecting any charges to be laid, so it is a surprise," he said. "But anyone who knows the facts about what happened would expect a police officer in any just society to be charged."
Given the time that has gone by, Prosper said he and other community groups had recently started planning to press authorities for details about the investigation. That won't be necessary now.
"It's a relief," he said. "Now we'll have to see what happens with the whole process."
Shortly after Jean-Pierre's death, activists started calling for a public, independent investigation and for police to release the name of the officer involved.

The incident occurred before the province's police-oversight bureau, the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), was operating. The bureau now investigates all incidents in which someone is killed or injured during a police intervention in Quebec.
Before the BEI was established, the protocol in place called for an outside police force to take over the cases. The investigation into Jean-Pierre's death was handled by the Sûreté du Québec.
